turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_te_zt_extrapolation_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Sb, O, Te, Co, Mg, Sn, Se, Pb, Si, S, Cu,
    Ge, Ni, Bi, Ti, Fe, Zn, In, Zr, Ca, Ag, T) and `target` (the measured zT
    measured at each row's own temperature T (K)).
  - b3_te_zt_extrapolation_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE samples whose zT at 800 K
    was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same
    process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST zT at 800
K, then select the 5 best candidates from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning

**1. Temperature trend in the training data.** Within nearly identical compositions the measured zT grows roughly linearly (often 2–3×) from 300 → 500 K, e.g.

| composition | 300 K | 400 K | 500 K |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sb₀.74Co₀.25 (CoSb₃) | 0.21–0.31 | 0.30–0.56 | 0.46–0.67 |
| Mg₀.67Sn₀.13Si₀.18(Ge,Bi) | 0.097 | 0.312 | 0.513 |
| Te₀.49Pb₀.49(Cu) | 0.225 | – | 0.727 |
| Sn/Ni/Ti/Zr half‑Heusler | 0.12–0.14 | 0.16–0.24 | 0.41–0.60 |
| Se₀.32Cu₀.65 (Cu₂Se) | 0.337 | – | 0.475–0.612 |

So the way to rank an 800 K extrapolation is: (i) identify the chemical family, (ii) take the best measured value of that family at 400–500 K, (iii) extend the family's slope, keeping in mind which families keep rising to 800 K (PbTe/PbTe–PbS, Cu₂Se, Mg₂(Si,Sn), skutterudites, half‑Heuslers) versus which are already flat/low (SnS, Ag₂Te, PbS, SnTe, oxides, Mg₂Si binary).

**2. Best-performing families in the training set (highest zT at 500 K):**
- Sb‑doped **PbTe** (Sb₀.036Te₀.50Pb₀.42 → **1.13 @500 K**; Sb₀.025Te₀.5Pb₀.45 → 0.96; Sb₀.012Te₀.50Pb₀.49 → 0.79; Te/Pb/Cu → 0.73) — the strongest and steepest family.
- PbTe–PbS / PbTe–Sb–S mixtures (0.37 @400 K).
- **Cu₂Se** (0.61 @500 K, rising fast).
- **Mg₂(Si,Sn)** solid solutions (0.50–0.70 @500 K, 0.43 @400 K).
- CoSb₃ skutterudites, Sb–Fe antimonides, Ti/Zr–Ni–Sn half‑Heuslers (0.4–0.67 @500 K).
- Low families: SnS (~0.02), pure Mg₂Si (~0.25–0.39), PbS (~0.19–0.25), SnTe (~0.05–0.10), Ca/Zn oxides (<0.05), Ag₂Te (~0.02), pure Ge (~0.1–0.36).

**3. Mapping the pool onto these families**

- **c043** = Sb₀.036Te₀.50Pb₀.415 — *identical* to the 1.13 @500 K training point; Sb‑doped PbTe peaks near 750–850 K → best expected (~1.6–2).
- **c046** = Sb₀.0075Te₀.50Pb₀.49 — lightly Sb‑doped PbTe, family value ~0.8–0.96 @500 K → ~1.3–1.5 @800 K.
- **c022** = Sb/Te₀.46Pb₀.49S₀.025Se — PbTe–PbS(Sb) alloy; the S‑alloyed PbTe rows rise steeply (0.095→0.37 from 300→400 K) → ~1.2–1.4.
- **c017** = Cu₀.66Se₀.34 — stoichiometric Cu₂Se, the family already at 0.47–0.61 @500 K and known to keep climbing → ~1.0–1.3. (c051 is the same but slightly In‑doped/off‑stoichiometric.)
- **c076 / c007 / c010** = Mg₂(Si,Sn)(Ge) solid solutions, 0.43–0.70 @400–500 K with a steep slope → ~1.0–1.2.
- CoSb₃ group (c061, c054, c003, c012, c072, c097) and Sb–Fe (c016, c015, c028) land around 0.8–1.1 — good but below the PbTe/Cu₂Se/Mg₂(Si,Sn) leaders.
- Clearly weak: SnS (c023, c055, c074, c079), oxides/Ca‑O (c008, c020, c042, c047, c070, c093), PbS (c092), SnTe (c001, c086, c095), Ag‑Te (c085), pure Mg₂Si (c041, c045, c090, c091), pure Ge (c026, c029, c059).

**4. Selection.** Take the two steepest, highest‑value families: Sb‑doped PbTe (and its S‑alloyed variant) plus Cu₂Se, then the best Mg₂(Si,Sn) alloy.

Final: c043, c046, c022, c017, c076
